title: Linear life cycles & why projects use phases
blurb: Name the four linear phases in order, explain why projects are split into phases with decision gates, and know when linear fits.
question: A water company is building a new treatment works to a design that regulators must approve. The sponsor insists on four phases with a formal decision gate between each. A board member asks why the work isn't simply planned and built in one go. What are the phases, and why does structuring the work this way make sense here?

teach.h: Plan it fully, then deliver to the plan
teach.body: A linear life cycle is a sequential life cycle: its phases are completed one after another, each building on the outputs of the last, with a decision gate between them. The APM Body of Knowledge names four phases: Concept, Definition, Deployment and Transition. In plain English: check it's worth doing, plan it properly, build it, then hand it over. Nobody starts building until the plan has been agreed.

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Is it worth doing? Need, options, outline business case

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: How exactly? Requirements, PMP, baseline, suppliers

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Build and test the outputs against the baseline

steps.label: Transition
steps.sub: Hand over to users and BAU, close, capture lessons

teach.caption: Decision gates (often called stage gates) sit BETWEEN phases. They are governance points, not phases.

teach.h: Why projects are structured as phases
items: Manageable chunks: a large, complex job is broken into stages the team can plan and control.
Control points: each gate lets the sponsor or board make a go or no-go decision and re-check the business case.
Progressive funding: money is released one phase at a time, not all on day one.
Risk management: the organisation commits step by step, so it can stop before the big spend if things change.
Clear deliverables: every phase has defined outputs that must be complete before the next begins.
Structure: phases give a framework for planning, reporting and assurance.

teach.h: What actually happens at a decision gate
teach.body: At the end of each phase the sponsor or steering group reviews the evidence: is the business case still justified, is the plan for the next phase ready, is funding available and are the risks acceptable? The outcome is to continue, to continue with conditions, to pause, or to close the project. Stopping a project that no longer makes sense is a success of governance, not a failure, because it protects money and effort that would otherwise be wasted.

teach.caption: Phasing lets you plan the next phase in detail once you know more, and commit larger sums only when estimates are firmer.
Phases follow in strict sequence. The big construction spend is only committed after Gate 2.

teach.body: In Concept, the water company confirmed the need and chose a new works over upgrading the old one. In Definition, a ground survey found contaminated land, and the estimate rose. At Gate 2 the board re-checked the business case, approved extra contingency and only then signed the construction contract. Had they built first and planned as they went, they would have discovered the problem with diggers already on site and money already spent.

teach.text: The linear phases are Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Feasibility and Foundations are ITERATIVE names, so any linear list containing them is wrong. Watch the order too: Definition (plan) always comes before Deployment (build). And a decision gate is a control point between phases, never a phase in its own right.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the phases in order: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition, separated by decision gates.
Explain the gates: go or no-go decisions where the business case, plans, funding and risks are re-checked.
Give the benefits of phasing: manageable stages, progressive funding, step-by-step commitment, clear deliverables.
Say when it fits: stable requirements, heavy regulation, costly late change (for example construction).
Apply it to the scenario in the question, not just in general terms.
Linear phases in order: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition.
Each phase is largely completed before the next starts; decision gates sit between them.
Phases give control points, progressive funding and step-by-step commitment of resources.
Linear suits stable requirements, regulation and work where late change is costly.
Gates can stop a project: closing an unjustified project early is good governance.

summary: You can now name the four linear phases in order and explain what each one produces. You can also explain why projects are structured as phases separated by decision gates, and recognise the situations where a linear life cycle is the right choice.

A.q: Which sequence correctly lists the phases of a linear life cycle?
A.why: The linear life cycle runs Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition: decide, plan, build, hand over.

whyNot.0: Deployment cannot come before Definition: the work is planned before it is built.
whyNot.1: Feasibility is the first phase of the ITERATIVE life cycle, not the linear one.
whyNot.3: Foundations is an ITERATIVE phase name; the second linear phase is Definition.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, where are decision gates positioned?
A.why: Decision gates sit between phases, so the project must pass a governance review before moving on.

whyNot.1: A gate at closure alone would remove the step-by-step control that phasing provides.
whyNot.2: Time boxes belong to iterative working; linear gates sit at phase ends.
whyNot.3: Benefits reviews happen after handover; decision gates control progress between phases.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate between linear phases?
options: To record lessons for the PMO
To hand outputs over to users
A.why: A gate is a go or no-go control point: the business case, plans, funding and risks are re-checked before the next phase is authorised.

whyNot.0: Lessons may be noted at a gate, but that is not its main purpose.
whyNot.1: Handing outputs to users is part of the Transition phase.
whyNot.3: Change requests go through change control whenever they arise, not only at gates.

B.q: A sponsor releases funding for Definition only, and will decide on Deployment funding at the next gate. Which benefit of phasing does this show?
options: Fixed time and cost per time box
B.why: Releasing money one phase at a time means the organisation commits step by step and can stop before the large spend.

whyNot.0: Fixed time and cost per time box is a feature of iterative working.
whyNot.1: Early usable value is a strength of iterative delivery, not of phased funding.
whyNot.2: Phasing does not remove change control; changes to the baseline still go through it.

B.q: In which linear phase would the detailed project management plan and baseline normally be produced?
B.why: Definition turns the approved concept into detailed requirements, the project management plan and the baseline for delivery.

whyNot.0: Concept establishes the need, options and outline business case, not the detailed plan.
whyNot.2: Deployment delivers the work against the baseline already set in Definition.
whyNot.3: Transition hands the outputs over and closes the project.

B.q: Which project is BEST suited to a linear life cycle?
options: A new hospital wing to a fixed design
A start-up app with unclear user needs
A research study into new materials
A website shaped by weekly user tests
B.why: A building to a fixed, approved design has stable requirements and very costly late change: the classic case for linear.

whyNot.1: Unclear user needs call for iterative working with frequent feedback.
whyNot.2: Exploratory research has uncertain outcomes, which suits an iterative approach.
whyNot.3: Weekly user testing that reshapes the product is iterative by nature.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for structuring a linear project into phases?
options: To commit resources step by step
To re-check the business case often
To let scope flex in fixed time boxes
To give each stage clear deliverables
C.why: Letting scope flex within fixed time boxes is an iterative feature. Linear phases fix the scope in a baseline and control change formally.

whyNot.0: Committing step by step is a core reason for phasing: it limits exposure if things change.
whyNot.1: Gates between phases are where the business case is re-checked.
whyNot.3: Each phase has defined outputs that must be complete before the next starts.

C.q: At the gate after Definition, a survey shows a new treatment works will cost far more than planned, with the same benefits. What should the gate review focus on?
options: Starting the build before costs rise
Cutting testing to stay in budget
Whether the case still justifies it
C.why: The gate exists to re-confirm the business case. Higher cost for the same benefits may still be justified, or may not; the board must decide before the major spend.

whyNot.0: Starting construction before the decision defeats the purpose of the gate and increases exposure.
whyNot.1: Transition is where outputs are handed over; skipping it would leave operations unprepared.
whyNot.2: Cutting testing trades quality for cost without asking whether the project is still worth doing.

C.q:
Which THREE are reasons projects are structured as phases?
1) Breaking work into manageable stages
2) Providing governance control points
3) Removing the need for a business case
4) Managing risk by committing step by step
C.why: Manageable stages, governance control points and step-by-step commitment are all reasons for phasing.

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: phasing relies on the business case, which is re-checked at every gate.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is false, and statement 2 (control points) is missing.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is false, and statement 1 (manageable stages) is missing.

reteach.title: Building a house extension
reteach.question: Imagine adding a kitchen extension to your home. Why would you never hire builders before you had drawings, planning permission and a price?

blocks.body: Concept: do we really need more space, and could we afford it? Definition: an architect draws plans, the council grants permission and builders quote a price. Deployment: the builders put up the walls and fit the kitchen. Transition: you check the work, pay the final invoice and move in. Before each step you pause and ask: is this still worth it? That pause is a decision gate.

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Do we need it? Can we afford it?

steps.label: Transition
steps.sub: Snag list, final payment, move in

blocks.text: If the quote comes back at twice your budget, the gate lets you stop before the walls come down. That is exactly why linear projects are phased: commit a little, learn, then decide.

explain.body: Concept asks whether the idea is worth pursuing: the need, the options and an outline business case. Definition works out exactly how: detailed requirements, the project management plan, the baseline and the choice of suppliers.

test.q: A team is comparing options and preparing an outline business case. Which linear phase are they in?
test.why: Comparing options and preparing the outline business case is the work of Concept, the first linear phase.

whyNot.0: Definition comes next: detailed requirements, plans and the baseline.
whyNot.1: Deployment is where the outputs are built.

explain.body: Deployment builds and tests the outputs, with progress measured against the baseline set in Definition. Transition hands the outputs to the users and business as usual, releases the team, closes the project and captures lessons.

test.q: Which activity belongs to the Transition phase of a linear life cycle?
test.why: Transition is where the outputs are handed over to users and BAU and the project is closed.

whyNot.0: The baseline is set in Definition.

explain.body: A decision gate (or stage gate) is a review point between phases where the sponsor or board decides whether to continue, continue with conditions, pause or close. It re-confirms the business case, the readiness of the next phase's plan, funding and risk.

test.q: At a decision gate, the board finds the business case no longer stands up. What is the most appropriate decision?
options: Ask the team to work faster
test.why: If the business case no longer holds, the gate exists to stop the project before more money is spent.

whyNot.1: Jumping to Transition would hand over incomplete outputs from an unjustified project.
whyNot.2: Continuing an unjustified project wastes resources; the gate is where it should be stopped.
whyNot.3: Working faster does not fix a business case that no longer justifies the project.

explain.body: Linear fits when requirements are stable and well defined, when regulation or safety demand formal sign-offs, and when late change is expensive, as in construction and engineering. It struggles when users cannot say what they need until they see it.

items.label: late change means rework or demolition

test.q: Which characteristic of a project most strongly suggests a linear life cycle?
options: Users want to shape it as it grows
Value is needed within a few weeks
The market is changing very quickly
test.why: Stable, agreed requirements let the whole project be planned and baselined up front, which is what linear relies on.

whyNot.0: Users shaping the solution as it grows calls for iterative feedback loops.
whyNot.2: Very early value is a reason to deliver incrementally (iterative).
whyNot.3: A fast-changing market makes fixed up-front requirements risky.
